html:
The copper statue of a robed woman holding up a torch, on an island in the harbour of New York, given by the people of France to the United States and dedicated on 28 October 1886.

The sculptor Frédéric Auguste Bartholdi designed it, and Gustave Eiffel, who later built the Eiffel Tower, made the iron frame that carries its thin copper skin. It was shipped in 350 pieces. The French paid for the statue and Americans for the pedestal, much of it through small gifts raised by a newspaper campaign. The figure is 46 metres tall, 93 metres with the pedestal, and the tablet in her hand bears the date of American independence, 4 July 1776. A broken chain lies at her feet.

It was the first sight of America for millions who arrived by ship and landed at nearby Ellis Island. A poem by Emma Lazarus, added on a plaque in 1903, gave it that meaning: "Give me your tired, your poor, your huddled masses yearning to breathe free."
sum: The copper statue of a robed woman holding up a torch, on an island in the harbour of New York, given by the people of France to the United States and dedicated on 28 October 1886.
